---
title: "Graphics gallery"
description: >
  Every figure the package draws, and how to adapt it for a paper, a slide
  or a report.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")
```

`autoplot()` and the `plot_*()` functions return ggplot objects. The
figures are ready for a manuscript as they are, and anything about them can
be changed with the usual ggplot2 grammar: add labels, scales, themes or
layers with `+`. This gallery shows each figure once, then the changes most
often needed before a figure goes into a paper or onto a slide.

The examples use three fits: tuberculosis mortality with empirical quantile
intervals (the default), all six causes of death in `us_mortality`, and the
prevalence of each body mass index category in `ontario_bmi`.

```{r fits}
library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)

tb <- subset(us_mortality, cause == "Tuberculosis")
fit_tb <- joinpoint(tb, year, rate, kmax = 3)

fit_all <- joinpoint(us_mortality, year, rate, by = "cause", kmax = 3,
                     ci_method = "parametric",
                     control = jp_control(aapc_last = 10))

fit_bmi <- joinpoint(ontario_bmi, year, count = count, population = births,
                     by = "category", type = "percent", kmax = 2,
                     method = "bic", ci_method = "parametric")
```

## Trend figures

`autoplot()` draws the observed values, the fitted model, the joinpoints and
the APC of each segment. `plot()` prints the same figure and returns the
fit, so use `autoplot()` to modify a figure.

### The default figure

The labels sit next to their segments and avoid each other and the fitted
curves.
An asterisk marks an APC that differs significantly from zero. The shaded
band is the pointwise 95% interval of the fitted curve; it is drawn when the
fit has empirical quantile intervals.

```{r default, fig.alt = "Tuberculosis death rate by year, 1900 to 1998, falling throughout, with the fitted joinpoint model, three joinpoints and the APC of each of the four segments."}
autoplot(fit_tb)
```

### Uncertainty on the figure

`labels = "ci"` writes the confidence interval under each APC, and
`joinpoint_ci = TRUE` shades the confidence interval of each joinpoint
location. Where a two-line label cannot be placed without overlapping
another label or a curve, it may be cut to the APC alone.

```{r uncertainty, fig.alt = "The tuberculosis figure with the confidence interval of each APC written under its label and gray bands showing the confidence intervals of the three joinpoint locations."}
autoplot(fit_tb, labels = "ci", joinpoint_ci = TRUE)
```

### Trend direction and a logarithmic axis

`color_by = "trend"` colors each segment by its direction: significantly
increasing, significantly decreasing or stable. On a logarithmic axis
(`log_y = TRUE`) equal percent changes have equal slopes, which suits
log-linear models. Several cohorts are drawn as panels, each with its own
scale; `ncol` sets the number of columns.

```{r trend, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Six panels, one per cause of death, on logarithmic axes, with segments colored by whether the trend increased, decreased or was stable."}
autoplot(fit_all, color_by = "trend", log_y = TRUE, ncol = 3)
```

### Several series in one panel

`layout = "overlay"` draws the cohorts in one panel, and `cohorts` picks
some of them by position. With `aapc = TRUE` each legend entry carries the
average annual percent change of the first AAPC range, the full range by
default. Segment labels are off
by default when series are overlaid, to keep the panel readable.

```{r overlay, fig.alt = "Death rates from heart disease, cancer and stroke in one panel on a logarithmic axis, with each legend entry giving the cause and its average annual percent change."}
levels(us_mortality$cause)
autoplot(fit_all, layout = "overlay", cohorts = c(2, 3, 5), aapc = TRUE,
         log_y = TRUE)
```

### Observed values with confidence intervals

When the data carry standard errors, given with `se` or calculated from
`count` and `population`, `error_bars = TRUE` adds the 95% interval of each
observed value.

```{r error-bars, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Six panels showing the yearly prevalence of each body mass index category in Ontario with 95% error bars and the fitted joinpoint models."}
autoplot(fit_bmi, error_bars = TRUE, ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = "Prevalence (%)")
```

### A model other than the selected one

`model` draws the best fitting model with a given number of joinpoints
instead of the selected one, for example to show a reviewer the simpler
alternative.

```{r other-model, fig.alt = "The tuberculosis series with the best fitting model with one joinpoint."}
autoplot(fit_tb, model = 1)
```

## Trend summaries

### APCs over time

`plot_apc()` draws the APC of every segment as a step over the years it
covers, with its confidence interval as a band and a reference line at
zero. It answers "how fast, and when" more directly than the data.

```{r apc, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Six panels showing the annual percent change of each segment as a horizontal step over the years it covers, with confidence bands and a dashed line at zero."}
plot_apc(fit_all, ncol = 3)
```

### AAPC forest plot

`plot_aapc()` compares average annual percent changes across cohorts and
ranges. The fit requested the last ten years in addition to the full range
through `jp_control(aapc_last = 10)`; custom ranges are set with
`aapc_ranges`.

```{r aapc, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Forest plot of the average annual percent change of each cause of death over the full range and over the last ten years, with confidence intervals."}
plot_aapc(fit_all)
```

## Model selection and diagnostics

### All candidate models

`plot_models()` shows the best fit for every number of joinpoints of one
cohort, with the selection statistic of each in its panel title and the
selected model highlighted. `overlay = TRUE` draws them in one panel.

```{r models, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Four small panels showing the best tuberculosis models with zero to three joinpoints, each titled with its selection statistic."}
plot_models(fit_tb, ncol = 2)
```

```{r models-overlay, fig.alt = "The four candidate tuberculosis models drawn over the data in one panel, with the selected model highlighted."}
plot_models(fit_tb, overlay = TRUE)
```

### Selection criteria

`plot_selection()` draws the selection statistic against the number of
joinpoints. For the permutation test it draws the sequence of tests
instead; `vignette("model-selection")` has an example.

```{r selection, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "The weighted BIC of the tuberculosis models with zero to three joinpoints."}
plot_selection(fit_tb)
```

### Residuals

`plot_residuals()` shows the standardized residuals of the selected model
against time, as a normal quantile plot, or as an autocorrelation function.
`vignette("uncertainty")` discusses what to do when neighboring residuals
are correlated.

```{r residuals, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Standardized residuals of the tuberculosis model plotted against year."}
plot_residuals(fit_tb)
```

```{r residuals-qq, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Normal quantile plot of the standardized residuals of the tuberculosis model."}
plot_residuals(fit_tb, type = "qq")
```

```{r residuals-acf, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Autocorrelation function of the standardized residuals of the tuberculosis model."}
plot_residuals(fit_tb, type = "acf")
```

## Comparing groups

`autoplot()` of a `jp_compare()` result draws the separately fitted models
(solid) and the model fitted under the null hypothesis (dashed), one panel
per pair. `vignette("comparing-groups")` explains the tests.

```{r compare, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Stroke and heart disease death rates with their separately fitted joinpoint models as solid lines and the jointly fitted parallel model as dashed lines."}
pair <- joinpoint(subset(us_mortality, cause %in% c("Stroke", "Heart Disease")),
                  year, rate, by = "cause", kmax = 2, ci_method = "parametric")
autoplot(jp_compare(pair, n_perm = 99), log_y = TRUE)
```

## Customizing the figures

### Titles, axis labels and captions

`labs()` replaces the automatic labels and adds a title and subtitle. A
caption given here replaces the automatic note that explains the labels,
band and error bars. `expression()` writes units with superscripts, as in
`y = expression("Mean BMI (kg/m"^2 * ")")`.

```{r labels, fig.alt = "The tuberculosis figure with a title, a subtitle, a source caption and custom axis labels."}
autoplot(fit_tb) +
  labs(title = "Tuberculosis mortality fell throughout the century",
       subtitle = "The decline was steepest from 1947, when streptomycin came into use",
       x = NULL, y = "Deaths per 100,000 (age adjusted)",
       caption = "Source: CDC National Vital Statistics System, HIST293.")
```

### Axes

The x axis is free to change. Breaks every twenty years, for example:

```{r x-axis, fig.alt = "The tuberculosis figure with x axis breaks every twenty years."}
autoplot(fit_tb) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2000, by = 20))
```

`autoplot()` sets the y scale itself, with room around the curves for the
segment labels, and ggplot2 notes when that scale is replaced. To change
the y axis, keep the room by passing the expansion `autoplot()` uses:
`mult = 0.12` with APC labels (the default), `0.2` with `labels = "ci"` and
`0.05` without labels.

```{r y-axis, message = FALSE, fig.alt = "The body mass index figure for obesity class III with y axis labels formatted as percentages."}
autoplot(fit_bmi, cohorts = 6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(v, "%"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0.12)) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = "Prevalence")
```

### Text size and fonts

`theme_joinpoint()` is the theme of every figure. Add it again with a larger
`base_size` for slides or a smaller one for a narrow journal column, and set
`base_family` to a font installed on your system.

```{r slides, fig.alt = "The tuberculosis figure with larger text for a slide."}
autoplot(fit_tb) + theme_joinpoint(base_size = 16)
```

Any complete ggplot2 theme works too, followed by `theme()` for details:

```{r other-theme, fig.alt = "The tuberculosis figure drawn with the ggplot2 classic theme."}
autoplot(fit_tb) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```

### Colors

The qualitative palette of `scale_color_joinpoint()` has eight colors,
ordered so that neighboring colors stay distinguishable under the common
forms of color vision deficiency. Use it in any ggplot2 figure, together
with `theme_joinpoint()`, to give your own figures the same look:

```{r palette, fig.alt = "Death rates of the six causes drawn as lines in the joinpoint palette and theme."}
ggplot(us_mortality, aes(year, rate, color = cause)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_joinpoint(name = NULL) +
  theme_joinpoint() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Deaths per 100,000")
```

To use other colors in a figure colored by cohort, replace the scale for
both the color and the fill aesthetics, since the fitted bands are filled
in the color of their cohort:

```{r manual-colors, message = FALSE, fig.alt = "Heart disease, cancer and stroke death rates in one panel drawn in custom colors."}
autoplot(fit_all, layout = "overlay", cohorts = c(2, 3, 5), log_y = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0B2540", "#2A78D6", "#7F8FA6"),
                     aesthetics = c("colour", "fill"), name = NULL)
```

### Figures built from the result tables

Every result is also a data frame, so any figure can be drawn from scratch.
`as.data.frame()` returns the observed and modeled values with the segment
and APC of each point, `joinpoints()` the joinpoint locations with their
intervals, and `apc()` the segment estimates. Here, the periods between
joinpoints are shaded and annotated with their APCs. The shaded rectangles
reach beyond the data and `coord_cartesian()` crops them to the panel, which
works on a logarithmic axis too:

```{r custom, fig.alt = "A custom figure of tuberculosis mortality on a logarithmic axis with each period between joinpoints shaded, the fitted line, and the APC of each period written at the top."}
pts <- as.data.frame(fit_tb)
seg <- apc(fit_tb)
seg$label <- sprintf("%.1f%%", seg$estimate)
lim <- range(pts$observed, pts$modeled)

ggplot(pts, aes(x)) +
  geom_rect(data = seg, aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = lim[1] / 10,
                            ymax = lim[2] * 10, fill = factor(segment %% 2)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.25, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed), color = "#7F8FA6", size = 1.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = modeled), color = "#2A78D6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = seg, aes(x = (start + end) / 2, y = Inf, label = label),
            vjust = 1.5, size = 3.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "#DCE8F7")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = lim) +
  theme_joinpoint() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Deaths per 100,000")
```

## Saving figures

`ggsave()` writes a figure at the size it will be printed. Journals usually
ask for widths of about 85 mm (one column) or 175 mm (two columns), at least
300 dpi for raster images, or a vector format such as PDF. Choose the size
first and set `base_size` to fit it, rather than scaling a large figure
down, so the text ends up at the intended size.

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
p <- autoplot(fit_tb) + theme_joinpoint(base_size = 9)
ggsave("tuberculosis.pdf", p, width = 85, height = 60, units = "mm")
ggsave("tuberculosis.png", p, width = 85, height = 60, units = "mm",
       dpi = 600, bg = "white")
```

Add alternative text to figures that are published online. In R Markdown and
Quarto documents, the `fig.alt` chunk option sets it, as on this page.
